input.prompt: Simulate the thermal conductivity of a Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluid using the Langevin thermostat method in LAMMPS. Define a simulation box with dimensions 10×10×20 in reduced LJ units and apply periodic boundary conditions in all directions. Set the number density of the fluid to 0.6 and the initial temperature to 1.35 in LJ units. Use a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice to initialize atomic positions and assign a Lennard-Jones potential with a cutoff of 2.5σ. Create two temperature-controlled regions: a hot region at the bottom (z = 0 to 1) and a cold region at the top (z = 10 to 11). First, equilibrate the system using the NVT ensemble at 1.35 for 1000 timesteps, then switch to the NVE ensemble while applying Langevin thermostats to the hot and cold regions to maintain temperatures at 1.70 and 1.0, respectively. Track the energy added and removed by the thermostats and compute the temperature difference between the regions. Run the simulation for 10,000 timesteps to establish a steady-state temperature gradient. Afterward, reset the Langevin energy accumulation and continue the simulation for an additional 20,000 timesteps while calculating the running average of the temperature difference. Divide the simulation box into bins along the z-direction and compute the temperature profile over time. Use the heat flux and steady-state temperature gradient to compute the thermal conductivity using Fourier’s law. As the final output, return the thermal conductivity κ in Lennard-Jones (LJ) reduced units.

Initialize a Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluid system in LAMMPS. Define a simulation box with dimensions 10×10×20 in reduced LJ units and apply periodic boundary conditions in all directions. Set the number density to 0.6 and the initial temperature to 1.35 in LJ units. Use a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice to distribute atoms within the box and assign atomic masses. Define a Lennard-Jones potential with a cutoff of 2.5σ. Assign initial velocities to the atoms according to a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at 1.35. Save this structure using the write_data command in LAMMPS data format. As the final output, return the absolute path of the structure file.

Equilibrate the Lennard-Jones fluid system in LAMMPS. Read the previously initialized structure file and apply periodic boundary conditions in all directions. Use the NVT ensemble to maintain the system at a constant temperature of 1.35 in LJ units with a damping parameter of 0.5. Run the equilibration for 1000 timesteps while monitoring system properties such as temperature. Save the state after this step. As the final output, return the absolute path of the updated structure file.

Stabilize the equilibrated Lennard-Jones fluid system in LAMMPS. Read the structure file from the previous equilibration step. Apply the NVE ensemble to evolve the system at constant energy. Use Langevin thermostats to control the temperature in two distinct regions: a hot region maintained at 1.70 in LJ units and a cold region maintained at 1.00 in LJ units, both with a damping parameter of 1.0. Assign the computed temperatures of these regions to separate temperature computes for monitoring. Modify the Langevin fixes to use these computed temperatures. Run the simulation for 10,000 timesteps while tracking temperature differences between the two regions. Save the final stabilized state. As the final output, return the absolute path of the updated structure file.

Read the stabilized system structure from the previous step. Apply Langevin thermostats to the hot and cold regions with target temperatures of 1.70 and 1.00, respectively. Use a damping parameter of 1.0. Define 1D binning along the z-direction with a bin size of 0.05. Compute a running average of the temperature difference and use it to calculate thermal conductivity. Run the simulation for 20,000 timesteps. As the final output, return the computed thermal conductivity value in Lennard-Jones (LJ) units.
